query: Rupnagar is a city in Punjab, India, known for its significance in the Indus Valley civilization. It features an archaeological museum showcasing artifacts from the Harappan period and has historical roots dating back to the 11th century.
answer:
### Rupnagar, Punjab, India

**Overview:**
Rupnagar, also known as Ropar, is a city and municipal council located in the Rupnagar district of Punjab, India. It is significant for its historical roots, particularly as one of the major sites of the Indus Valley civilization. The city is approximately 47 km northwest of Chandigarh and serves as a divisional headquarters comprising Rupnagar, Mohali, and its adjoining districts.

**Historical Significance:**
- **Indus Valley Civilization:** Rupnagar is one of the larger archaeological sites associated with the Indus Valley civilization. It features an archaeological museum that exhibits artifacts from the Harappan period, including antiquities and coins from ancient times.
- **Etymology:** The city is said to have been named by a Raja named Rokeshar in the 11th century, after his son Rup Sen.

**Attractions:**
- **Archaeological Museum:** Opened in 1998, the museum showcases the archaeological remains from the excavated site, marking it as the first Harappan site of Independent India. The exhibits include artifacts from various periods, revealing a cultural sequence from the Harappan to medieval times.

**Visual Tags:**
- Cityscape
- Attraction
- Museum

**Further Information:**
For more details, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Rupnagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupnagar).

If you have any specific questions or need more information about Rupnagar, feel free to ask!

(August 2023) (Learn how and when to remove this message) Shillong was the capital of composite Assam during the British regime and for a quarter century in independent India until a separate State of Meghalaya was formed 1972. David Scott, the British civil servant of the East India Company, was the Agent of the Governor-General North East Frontier. During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British authorities felt the need for a road to connect Sylhet and Assam. The route was to traverse across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott overcame the difficulties his administration faced from the opposition of the Khasi Syiems – their chiefs and people. Impressed by the favourable cool climate of Khasi Hills, they negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra in 1829 for a sanatorium for the British. Thus began the consolidation of British interests in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills. In early 1829, a Khasis confederation mounted a serious uprising against British occupation. But by January 1833, their leader Tirot Sing surrendered to David Scott and was detained to Dacca (present-day Dhaka). A political agent was posted in Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee. But the British did not like the climate and facilities of Sohra and they moved to Shillong. "Ïewduh" is the biggest market in Shillong. The name "Shillong" was later adopted, as the location of the new town was below the Shillong Peak. In 1874, a separate Chief Commissionership was formed with Shillong as the seat of administration. The new administration included Sylhet, now a part of Bangladesh. Also included in the Chief Commissionership were the Naga Hills (present-day Nagaland), Lushai Hills (present-day Mizoram) as well as Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. Shillong was the capital of composite Assam till 1969 when the autonomous state of Meghalaya was formed. In January 1972, Meghalaya was made a full-fledged state.[1] The Shillong Municipal Board dates back to 1878, when a proclamation was issued constituting Shillong and its suburbs, including the villages of Mawkhar and Laban, into a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876. Inclusion of the villages of Mawkhar (S.E. Mawkhar, Jaiaw and part of Jhalupara and Mawprem) and Laban (Lumparing, Madan laban, Kench's Trace and Rilbong) within the Municipality of Shillong was agreed to by Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem under the agreement of 15 November 1878.[2] But, there is no trace of Shillong in the British era maps dating back to 1878, up to 1900. answer:
### Beijing Ancient Observatory (北京古观象台)

- **Location**: Beijing, China
- **Category**: Attraction
- **Popularity**: 0.7

#### Historical Summary
The Beijing Ancient Observatory is a pretelescopic observatory located in Beijing, China. Built in 1442 during the Ming dynasty, it was expanded during the Qing dynasty. The observatory underwent significant reorganization and received many new, more accurate instruments from European Jesuit astronomers in 1644. It played a crucial role in the observation of celestial bodies for the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties.

#### Access and Nearby Attractions
The observatory is located just south of Jianguomen in Dongcheng District. It can be accessed via Lines 1 and 2 of the Beijing Subway to Jianguomen station (Exit C) and several bus routes. Nearby attractions include the Beijing railway station and the Ming City Wall Relics Park.

#### Additional Information
- **Wikipedia**: [Beijing Ancient Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Ancient_Observatory)
- **Visual Tags**: Exterior, cityscape, China

This historic site is a must-visit for those interested in astronomy and the history of science in China.

wikipedia.extract_text: The Beijing Ancient Observatory is a pretelescopic observatory located in Beijing, China. The observatory was built in 1442 during the Ming dynasty, and expanded during the Qing. It received major reorganization and many new, more accurate instruments from Europeans (Jesuits) in 1644.

sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] An image of the observatory after reorganization by the Jesuits The layout of the observatory It was said that in 1227, the Jin dynasty transferred the ancient astronomical instruments from Kaifeng to the first observatory in Beijing. In 1279, the succeeding Mongols under Kublai Khan built a new observatory just north of the current observatory. Kublai Khan made his chief adviser of hydraulics, mathematics and astronomy, Guo Shoujing, director of the observatory in 1283 after the death of Guo's friend and predecessor Zhang Wenqian.[1] After the Mongols, Zhu Yuanzhang, the founding Ming Emperor, transferred the instruments from Beijing to Nanjing. When the Yongle Emperor came to power, he had craftsmen make copies of the instruments in Nanjing and sent them to the Beijing observatory. The current observatory was completed in 1442. It assisted the Ming and Qing astronomers in their observation reports for the Emperor. As he was considered the "Son of Heaven", the movements of the heavenly bodies were an important affair. Another function was to assist sea navigation, with Muslim scholars recruited for their expertise in the area.[citation needed] In the mid-17th century, after winning an astronomy contest, the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest was awarded complete charge of the astronomy observatory by the emperor. In 1673, he supervised the rebuilding of some of the instruments. He and other Jesuits helped to further develop the observations of the stars and the planets. During the later stages of the Qing dynasty, members of the Eight-Nation Alliance looted some of the instruments. However, as World War I drew to a close, the instruments were returned to China by the French and German governments. An early seismograph of Zhang Heng's design used to be housed at the observatory. Some of the instruments from the Ming era are now at Purple Mountain Observatory in Nanjing.[2][3] ^ .mw-parser-output cite.citation{font-style:inherit;word-wrap:break-word}.mw-parser-output .citation query: 大水法, located in Beijing's Yuanmingyuan, features a group of fountains set against a Western-style architectural backdrop. It was designed to blend Chinese and Western architectural styles during the Qing Dynasty.
answer:
The **大水法 (Great Fountain)** is located in the northern part of the Changchun Garden within the Yuanmingyuan (Old Summer Palace) in Beijing, China. This attraction features a series of fountains set against a backdrop of Western-style architectural elements. 

### Key Information:
- **Historical Significance**: Designed during the Qing Dynasty, specifically around 1759, the Great Fountain was intended to blend Chinese and Western architectural styles. The term "水法" (water method) referred to artificial fountains during the Qing period, hence the name.
- **Architecture**: The structure showcases a unique combination of Western-style stone niches and traditional Chinese elements, reflecting the cultural exchange of the time.
- **Popularity**: It is recognized as a significant tourist attraction, with a popularity score of 0.7.

### Additional Resources:
For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A7%E6%B0%B4%E6%B3%95).

If you have any more questions or need further assistance, feel free to ask!

wikipedia.title: 성산일출봉
wikipedia.extract: Seongsan Ilchulbong (Korean: 성산일출봉), also called Sunrise Peak, is a volcano on eastern Jeju Island, in Seongsan-ri, Seogwipo, Jeju Province, South Korea. It is 182 meters high and has a volcanic crater at the top.
wikipedia.extract_text: Seongsan Ilchulbong (Korean: 성산일출봉), also called Sunrise Peak, is a volcano on eastern Jeju Island, in Seongsan-ri, Seogwipo, Jeju Province, South Korea. It is 182 meters high and has a volcanic crater at the top.

sections.title: Description
sections.content: Description[edit] In 2021, a study reported that a 600 m (2,000 ft) wide crater from before the formation of Seongsan Ilchulbong now partially overlaps with the mountain site.[1] View of the mountain from space (2015) Seongsan Ilchulbong was formed around 6,700 years ago,[2] by Surtseyan-type hydrovolcanic activity upon a shallow seabed.[3][2] The earliest eruption related to the peak occurred around 600 m (2,000 ft) to the east of the current crater. After the eruption stopped, magma could not flow through that spot, which caused magma to later emerge at the location of the peak. Over time, most of the early cones and parts of the later tuff cone were eroded by waves, leaving parts of the internal structure exposed along the cliffs.[4] The mountain was originally disconnected from Jeju Island, but the accumulation of sediment caused the two to connect.[4][5] The mountain is considered to be geologically interesting and is actively studied by volcanologists.[6][5] The mountain is 182 m (597 ft) tall and has a diameter of 600 m (2,000 ft). It has a grassy volcanic crater at the top with a smooth, shallow bowl shape. The crater has an area of 2.64 km2 (1.02 mi2) and is around 90 m (300 ft) above sea level.[5] A 2011 study reported that there are 240 taxa of plant species on the mountain.[7] ^ .mw-parser-output sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] During the Goryeo under Mongol rule period (13th to 14th centuries), ranches for horses were established near the mountain.[1] During the 1910–1945 Japanese colonial period and near the end of World War II, the Imperial Japanese Navy dug caves into the sides of the mountain [ko], where they stashed boats loaded with explosives. These boats were intended to stymie anticipated Allied landings on Jeju; the around 18 caves they dug remain, and are now Registered Cultural Heritages of South Korea.[2][3][1] In the 20th century, farmers reportedly grew bamboo in the crater.[4] People raised horses and lived inside the crater before it became an environmentally protected site in the late 20th century.[1] ^ a b c Cite error: query: Deekshabhoomi is a sacred monument of Navayana Buddhism located in Nagpur, India, where B. R. Ambedkar and approximately 400,000 followers embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956. It symbolizes the revival of Buddhism in India and is significant for the Dalit Buddhist movement.
answer:
### Deekshabhoomi Overview

**Name:** Deekshabhoomi (दीक्षाभूमी)

**Location:** Nagpur, Maharashtra, India

**Category:** Monument / Attraction

**Historical Significance:**
Deekshabhoomi is a sacred monument of Navayana Buddhism located in Nagpur, where B. R. Ambedkar, along with approximately 400,000 followers, embraced Buddhism on October 14, 1956. This event marked a significant moment in the revival of Buddhism in India and is particularly important for the Dalit Buddhist movement.

**Key Facts:**
- **Date of Conversion:** October 14, 1956
- **Significance:** Symbolizes the mass conversion of Dalits to Buddhism and the efforts to abandon the caste system.
- **Architectural Features:** The site includes a stupa and is designed to commemorate the mass conversion ceremony led by Ambedkar.

**Further Reading:**
For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Deekshabhoomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deekshabhoomi).

**Visual Tags:** The site is recognized for its exterior, panoramic views, and is categorized as a temple and monument.

This monument not only serves as a place of worship but also as a symbol of social justice and equality, reflecting the aspirations of the Dalit community in India.

If you have any more questions or need further information, feel free to ask!

sections.content: History[edit] .mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+link+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}See also: Dalit Buddhist movement and Navayana Ambedkar delivering speech during mass conversion in Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, 14 October 1956. Dr. Ambedkar had declared in 1935 that although he was born as a Hindu, he would not die as one,[1] as conversion was the solution to abandon the caste system.[2] After this declaration and having extensively and exhaustively studied the doctrines of all the major world religions, Dr. Ambedkar would choose Buddhism for himself and his followers.[2] Buddhism was 2,550 years old in 1956, so it was a notable year of celebration for the Buddhist religious world globally and 14 October was the traditional date of conversion of Emperor Ashoka, the great Indian Buddhist Monarch and the day is celebrated as Ashok Vijaya Dashmi.[3] He selected Nagpur for his conversion ceremony, as he explained in his speech at that occasion, because Nagpur was the homeland of 'Nag' people who embraced Buddhism, supported it with great efforts in its early period, and propagated it throughout India.[4][5] Ground near the Ramdaspeth area in Nagpur was selected for the ceremony. On 14 October 1956, Dr. Ambedkar and his wife took the oath of Three Jewels and Five Precepts from the Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani from Kushinagar.[6][7] Dr. Ambedkar then gave the oath of Three Jewels, Five Precepts, and 22 Vows to thousands of his followers.[6] In this way, Nagpur became the birthplace of Neo Buddhist movement.[8] Dr. Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956, one and a half months after the Deeksha ceremony. However, this ceremonial conversion continued after his death, converting 15-20 million by March 1959.[9] After his death the 'Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Smarak Samiti' (Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee) was organized for the management of Deekshabhoomi. The committee decided to build a stupa at the place as a monument of that ceremony and a mass conversion of people to Buddhism. Arya Bhadant Surai Sasai is the president of the Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee, Nagpur.[10][11] ^ .mw-parser-output sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] .mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+link+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}See also: Dalit Buddhist movement and Navayana Ambedkar delivering speech during mass conversion in Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, 14 October 1956. Dr. Ambedkar had declared in 1935 that although he was born as a Hindu, he would not die as one,[1] as conversion was the solution to abandon the caste system.[2] After this declaration and having extensively and exhaustively studied the doctrines of all the major world religions, Dr. Ambedkar would choose Buddhism for himself and his followers.[2] Buddhism was 2,550 years old in 1956, so it was a notable year of celebration for the Buddhist religious world globally and 14 October was the traditional date of conversion of Emperor Ashoka, the great Indian Buddhist Monarch and the day is celebrated as Ashok Vijaya Dashmi.[3] He selected Nagpur for his conversion ceremony, as he explained in his speech at that occasion, because Nagpur was the homeland of 'Nag' people who embraced Buddhism, supported it with great efforts in its early period, and propagated it throughout India.[4][5] Ground near the Ramdaspeth area in Nagpur was selected for the ceremony. On 14 October 1956, Dr. Ambedkar and his wife took the oath of Three Jewels and Five Precepts from the Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani from Kushinagar.[6][7] Dr. Ambedkar then gave the oath of Three Jewels, Five Precepts, and 22 Vows to thousands of his followers.[6] In this way, Nagpur became the birthplace of Neo Buddhist movement.[8] Dr. Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956, one and a half months after the Deeksha ceremony. However, this ceremonial conversion continued after his death, converting 15-20 million by March 1959.[9] After his death the 'Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Smarak Samiti' (Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee) was organized for the management of Deekshabhoomi. The committee decided to build a stupa at the place as a monument of that ceremony and a mass conversion of people to Buddhism. Arya Bhadant Surai Sasai is the president of the Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee, Nagpur.[10][11] ^ .mw-parser-output ### Shorsky National Park Overview

- **Name**: Шорский национальный парк (Shorsky National Park)
- **Location**: Southwestern Siberia, Russia, covering a significant portion of the Tashtagolsky District in Kemerovo Oblast.
- **Established**: 1999
- **Area**: Approximately 1,614 square miles (4,180 km²).
- **Category**: National Park, protected area.

### Description
Shorsky National Park is characterized by its forested, mountainous terrain and dark taiga tree cover. It is situated where the West Siberian Plain meets the South Siberian Mountains, making it a representative area of this unique ecosystem. The park is home to the indigenous Shors people, who have historically been associated with the region's mining and logging industries.

### Historical Context
The area has been inhabited by the Shors people, known for their iron-smelting skills and practices of Shamanism. Active logging in the area ceased after the park's establishment, allowing the mature forest to thrive.

### Visual Tags
- **Season**: Summer
- **Tags**: Mountain, park, aerial views, ground level, sunny, spring greenery, summer lush.

### Popularity
The park has a popularity score of 0.7, indicating it is a well-regarded destination for visitors.

### Additional Information
For more details, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shorsky_National_Park).

If you're planning a visit, summer is considered the best season to explore the lush landscapes of Shorsky National Park!

answer:
### Final Information on Hukou Waterfall (壶口瀑布)

- **Description**: Hukou Waterfall is the largest waterfall on the Yellow River, the second largest waterfall in China, and the world's largest yellow waterfall. It is located at the intersection of Shanxi and Shaanxi provinces in China, approximately 165 km (103 mi) west of Fenxi County and 50 km (31 mi) east of Yichuan County. The width of the waterfall varies with the seasons, typically around 30 meters (98 ft) but can increase to 50 meters (164 ft) during flood season. The waterfall has a height of over 20 meters (66 ft).

- **Geographical Features**: As the Yellow River approaches Hukou Mountain, its width is narrowed by mountains on both sides, causing the water's velocity to increase before plunging over a cliff, creating a waterfall that appears as if water is pouring from a giant teapot.

- **Visual Tags**: The waterfall is surrounded by a valley and mountains, and it can be seen in various weather conditions, including sunny and cloudy days.

- **Popularity**: It has a popularity score of 0.7, indicating it is a well-known tourist attraction.

- **Further Information**: For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Hukou Waterfalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukou_Waterfalls).

If you have any specific questions or need further details, feel free to ask!

query: The Pak Ou Caves are a group of two caves located near the Mekong River, about 25 km north of Luang Prabang, Laos. They are popular tourist destinations, often visited for their scenic views and cultural significance.
answer:
The **Pak Ou Caves** are a notable tourist attraction located near the Mekong River, approximately 25 km north of Luang Prabang, Laos. These caves, known as Tham Ting and Tham Theung, are famous for their scenic views and cultural significance. They are situated on the west side of the Mekong River and are frequently visited by tourists, often taking about two hours to reach from the center of Luang Prabang.

### Key Information:
- **Location**: Near Pak Ou, 25 km north of Luang Prabang, Laos
- **Caves**: Tham Ting and Tham Theung
- **Category**: Attraction
- **Popularity**: Moderate (0.7)
- **Cultural Significance**: The caves are known for their historical and cultural importance, often featuring numerous Buddha statues.

For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Pak Ou Caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pak_Ou_Caves).

If you're planning a visit, expect a beautiful journey along the Mekong River, with opportunities to explore the caves and enjoy the surrounding natural beauty.

query: Seongsan Ilchulbong, also known as Sunrise Peak, is a volcanic formation on Jeju Island, South Korea. It features a grassy crater and is geologically significant, attracting the interest of volcanologists.
answer:
### Seongsan Ilchulbong (Sunrise Peak)

- **Location**: Eastern Jeju Island, Seongsan-ri, Seogwipo, Jeju Province, South Korea
- **Height**: 182 meters
- **Type**: Volcanic formation with a grassy crater at the top
- **Geological Significance**: Formed approximately 6,700 years ago through hydrovolcanic activity. The mountain is considered geologically interesting and is studied by volcanologists.

#### Description
Seongsan Ilchulbong, also known as Sunrise Peak, features a volcanic crater that is about 600 meters wide and has a diameter of 600 meters. The crater is approximately 90 meters above sea level and covers an area of 2.64 km². The site is rich in biodiversity, with around 240 taxa of plant species documented.

#### Historical Context
During the Goryeo period, ranches for horses were established near the mountain. In the 20th century, particularly during the Japanese colonial period, caves were dug into the mountain by the Imperial Japanese Navy, which are now recognized as Registered Cultural Heritage sites in South Korea.

#### Tourism
Seongsan Ilchulbong is a popular tourist attraction, especially known for its stunning sunrise views. The area is often visited for hiking and enjoying the panoramic coastal scenery.

#### Additional Information
- **Wikipedia**: [Seongsan Ilchulbong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seongsan_Ilchulbong)
- **Visual Tags**: Mountain, Island, Aerial, Sunny, Coast, Panoramic

This viewpoint is a must-see for visitors to Jeju Island, offering both natural beauty and cultural significance.

sections.content: Description[edit] In 2021, a study reported that a 600 m (2,000 ft) wide crater from before the formation of Seongsan Ilchulbong now partially overlaps with the mountain site.[1] View of the mountain from space (2015) Seongsan Ilchulbong was formed around 6,700 years ago,[2] by Surtseyan-type hydrovolcanic activity upon a shallow seabed.[3][2] The earliest eruption related to the peak occurred around 600 m (2,000 ft) to the east of the current crater. After the eruption stopped, magma could not flow through that spot, which caused magma to later emerge at the location of the peak. Over time, most of the early cones and parts of the later tuff cone were eroded by waves, leaving parts of the internal structure exposed along the cliffs.[4] The mountain was originally disconnected from Jeju Island, but the accumulation of sediment caused the two to connect.[4][5] The mountain is considered to be geologically interesting and is actively studied by volcanologists.[6][5] The mountain is 182 m (597 ft) tall and has a diameter of 600 m (2,000 ft). It has a grassy volcanic crater at the top with a smooth, shallow bowl shape. The crater has an area of 2.64 km2 (1.02 mi2) and is around 90 m (300 ft) above sea level.[5] A 2011 study reported that there are 240 taxa of plant species on the mountain.[7] ^ .mw-parser-output sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] During the Goryeo under Mongol rule period (13th to 14th centuries), ranches for horses were established near the mountain.[1] During the 1910–1945 Japanese colonial period and near the end of World War II, the Imperial Japanese Navy dug caves into the sides of the mountain [ko], where they stashed boats loaded with explosives. These boats were intended to stymie anticipated Allied landings on Jeju; the around 18 caves they dug remain, and are now Registered Cultural Heritages of South Korea.[2][3][1] In the 20th century, farmers reportedly grew bamboo in the crater.[4] People raised horses and lived inside the crater before it became an environmentally protected site in the late 20th century.[1] ^ a b c Cite error: sections.content: History[edit] During the Goryeo under Mongol rule period (13th to 14th centuries), ranches for horses were established near the mountain.[1] During the 1910–1945 Japanese colonial period and near the end of World War II, the Imperial Japanese Navy dug caves into the sides of the mountain [ko], where they stashed boats loaded with explosives. These boats were intended to stymie anticipated Allied landings on Jeju; the around 18 caves they dug remain, and are now Registered Cultural Heritages of South Korea.[2][3][1] In the 20th century, answer:
**Gangotri** is a town located in the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, India. It is a significant Hindu pilgrimage site situated on the banks of the river Bhagirathi, which is recognized as the origin of the Ganges River. The town is positioned in the Greater Himalayan Range at an elevation of 3,100 meters (10,200 feet).

### Key Information:
- **Category**: Attraction
- **Popularity**: Moderate (0.7)
- **Historical Significance**: According to Hindu legend, the goddess Ganga descended at this location when Lord Shiva released the river from his hair.

### Additional Details:
- **Distance**: Gangotri is approximately 99 km from Uttarkashi, the main district headquarters.
- **Visual Tags**: The area is known for its mountainous terrain, temples, and panoramic views, often attracting hikers and tourists.

For more information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Gangotri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangotri).

result.llm_sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ve.viewpoint_id, 
                ve.name_primary, 
                ve.name_variants, 
                ve.category_norm, 
                ve.popularity, 
                1.0 AS name_score,

                1.0 AS category_score

query: The Mogao Caves, also known as the Thousand Buddha Grottoes, are a system of 500 temples located near Dunhuang, China. They were constructed starting in the 4th century AD and are renowned for their exquisite Buddhist art and frescoes, making them one of the largest repositories of Buddhist art in the world.
answer:
### Mogao Caves (莫高窟)

- **Location**: 25 km southeast of Dunhuang, Gansu province, China.
- **Also Known As**: Thousand Buddha Grottoes or Caves of the Thousand Buddhas.
- **Description**: The Mogao Caves are a system of 500 temples renowned for their exquisite Buddhist art and frescoes, spanning over 1,000 years of history. They are one of the largest repositories of Buddhist art in the world.

#### Historical Significance
- The caves were first constructed in the 4th century AD and served as a site of Buddhist worship and pilgrimage.
- Dunhuang was established as a frontier garrison outpost by the Han dynasty and became a crucial gateway along the Silk Road.
- The site contains over 400,000 square feet of frescoes and sculptures, showcasing the evolution of Buddhist art.

#### Key Features
- The Mogao Caves contain some of the finest examples of Buddhist art, with intricate murals and sculptures.
- They were initially used by hermit monks for meditation and later developed into a significant pilgrimage site.

#### Additional Information
- The caves are also referred to as the Dunhuang Caves, although this term can include other nearby Buddhist cave sites.
- The site has been a focus of interest for Western explorers since the late 19th century, leading to its revival and preservation.

For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Mogao Caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogao_Caves).

If you have any further questions or need additional information, feel free to ask!

wikipedia.title: 莫高窟
wikipedia.extract: The Mogao Caves, also known as the Thousand Buddha Grottoes or Caves of the Thousand Buddhas, form a system of 500 temples 25 km (16 mi) southeast of the center of Dunhuang, an oasis located at a religious and cultural crossroads on the Silk Road, in Gansu province, China. The caves may also be known as the Dunhuang Caves; however, this term is also used as a collective term to include other Buddhist cave sites in and around the Dunhuang area, such as the Western Thousand Buddha Caves, Eastern Thousand Buddha Caves, Yulin Caves, and Five Temple Caves. The caves contain some of the finest examples of Buddhist art spanning a period of 1,000 years.

sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] Dunhuang was established as a frontier garrison outpost by the Han dynasty Emperor Wudi to protect against the Xiongnu in 111 BC. It also became an important gateway to the West, a centre of commerce along the Silk Road, as well as a meeting place of various people and religions such as Buddhism. The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang were first constructed in the 4th century AD and were used as a site of Buddhist worship and pilgrimage. The caves contain over 400,000 square feet of frescoes and sculptures, making them one of the largest repositories of Buddhist art in the world.[1] The construction of the Mogao Caves is generally taken to have begun sometime in the fourth century AD, when Dunhuang was under control of the Former Liang dynasty. According to a book written during the reign of Tang Empress Wu, Fokan Ji (佛龕記, An Account of Buddhist Shrines) by Li Junxiu (李君修), a Buddhist monk named Le Zun (樂尊, which may also be pronounced Yuezun) had a vision of a thousand Buddhas bathed in golden light at the site in 366 AD, inspiring him to build a cave here.[2] The story is also found in other sources, such as in inscriptions on a stele in cave 332; an earlier date of 353 however was given in another document, Shazhou Tujing (沙州土鏡, Geography of Shazhou).[3] He was later joined by a second monk Faliang (法良), and the site gradually grew, by the time of the Northern Liang a small community of monks had formed at the site. The caves initially served only as a place of meditation for hermit monks, but developed to serve the monasteries that sprang up nearby. The earliest decorated Mogao Caves remaining to this day (caves 268, 272 and 275), were built and decorated in the Northern Liang period between 419 and 439 CE, before the invasion of the Northern Wei. They share many stylistic characteristics in common with some of the Kizil Caves, such as Cave 17.[4][5] Members of the ruling family of Northern Wei and Northern Zhou then constructed many caves here, and it flourished in the short-lived Sui dynasty. By the Tang dynasty, the number of caves had reached over a thousand.[6] Details of painting of the meeting of Manjusri and Vimalakirti. Cave 159. By the Sui and Tang dynasties, Mogao Caves had become a place of worship and pilgrimage for the public.[7] From the 4th until the 14th century, caves were constructed by monks to serve as shrines with funds from donors. These caves were elaborately painted, the cave paintings and architecture serving as aids to meditation, as visual representations of the quest for enlightenment, as mnemonic devices, and as teaching tools to inform those illiterate about Buddhist beliefs and stories. The major caves were sponsored by patrons such as important clergy, local ruling elite, foreign dignitaries, as well as Chinese emperors. Other caves may have been funded by merchants, military officers, and other local people such as women's groups. During the Tang dynasty, Dunhuang became the main hub of commerce of the Silk Road and a major religious centre. A large number of the caves were constructed at Mogao during this era, including the two large statues of Buddha at the site, the largest one constructed in 695 following an edict a year earlier by Tang Empress Wu Zetian to build giant statues across the country.[8] The site escaped the persecution of Buddhists ordered by Emperor Wuzong in 845 as it was then under Tibetan control. As a frontier town, Dunhuang had been occupied at various times by other non-Han Chinese people. After the Tang dynasty, the site went into a gradual decline, and construction of new caves ceased entirely after the Yuan dynasty. By then Islam had conquered much of Central Asia, and the Silk Road declined in importance when trading via sea-routes began to dominate Chinese trade with the outside world. During the Ming dynasty, the Silk Road was finally officially abandoned, and Dunhuang slowly became depopulated and largely forgotten by the outside world. Most of the Mogao caves were abandoned; the site, however, was still a place of pilgrimage and was used as a place of worship by local people at the beginning of the twentieth century when there was renewed interest in the site. Discovery and revival[edit] Bodhisattva leading a lady donor towards the Pure Lands. Painting on silk (Library Cave), Late Tang. Dhaulagiri, located in Nepal, is the seventh highest mountain in the world at 8,167 metres (26,795 ft) above sea level, and the highest mountain within the borders of a single country. sections.content: History[edit] 1809 - Captain William Webb calibrated the height [1] Climbing history[edit] The unclimbed South Face of Dhaulagiri, seen from Poon Hill Dhaulagiri I in October 2002. The northeast ridge is the left skyline. Dhaulagiri was the penultimate eight-thousander to be summitted, and the final in Nepal. As its other routes are disproportionately dangerous, most ascents have followed the Northeast Ridge route of the first ascent, but climbs have been made from most directions. As of 2024, the two aspects which have repelled all attempts along their full length are the Northwest Ridge (though it has been climbed to the summit via the so-called "Pear" buttress) and the South Face. The latter is often regarded as one of the greatest remaining challenges in alpinism. As of 2007, there had been 358 successful ascents and 58 fatalities, which is a summit to a fatality rate of 16.2%.[2] Between 1950 and 2006, 2.88% of 2,016 expedition members and staff going above base camp on Dhaulagiri I died. On all 8,000 metre peaks in Nepal the death rate was 1.63%, ranging from 0.65% on Cho Oyu to 4.04% on Annapurna I and 3.05% on Manaslu.[3] Partial timeline[edit] 1950 – Dhaulagiri I reconnoitered by a French expedition led by Maurice Herzog. They do not see a feasible route and switch to Annapurna, where they make the first ascent of an 8000 m peak.[4] 1953–1958 – Five expeditions attempt the north face, or "Pear Buttress", route. 1959 – Austrian expedition led by Fritz Moravec makes the first attempt on the northeast ridge.[5] 1960 – Swiss-Austrian expedition led by Max Eiselin, successful ascent by Kurt Diemberger, Peter Diener, Ernst Forrer, Albin Schelbert, Nyima Dorje Sherpa, Nawang Dorje Sherpa on 13 May.[6] First Himalayan climb supported by the first prototype fixed-wing aircraft, which, after establishing the still standing record for highest fixed wing landing, eventually crashed in Hidden Valley north of the mountain during takeoff and was abandoned.[7] 1969 – American team led by Boyd Everett attempt southeast ridge; seven team members, including Everett, were killed in an avalanche.[8] 1970 – The second ascent, via the northeast ridge by a Japanese expedition led by Tokufu Ohta and Shoji Imanari. Tetsuji Kawada and Lhakpa Tenzing Sherpa reach the summit.[9] 1973 – American team led by James D. Morrissey makes the third ascent via the northeast ridge. Summit team: John Roskelley, Louis Reichardt, and Nawang Samden Sherpa.[10] 1975 – Japanese team led by Takashi Amemiya attempts southwest ridge (also known as the south pillar). Six are killed in an avalanche, including Norio Suzuki.[11] 1976 – Italian expedition makes the fourth ascent. 1977 – International team led by Reinhold Messner attempts the south face. 1978, spring: Amemiya returns with an expedition that puts five members on the summit via the southwest ridge—the first ascent not using the northeast ridge. One team member dies during the ascent. 1978, autumn – Seiko Tanaka of Japan leads successful climb of the very difficult southeast ridge. Four are killed during the ascent. French team attempts the southwest buttress (also called the "south buttress"), only reaches 7,200 m. 1980 – A four-man team consisting of Polish climbers Voytek Kurtyka, Ludwik Wiczyczynski, Frenchman René Ghilini, and Scotsman Alex MacIntyre climb the east face, topping out at 7,500 m on the northeast ridge. After a bivouac, they descend back to base camp in a storm. One week later they climb the mountain via the northeast ridge reaching the summit on 18 May.[12] 1981 – Yugoslav team reaches 7,950 m after putting up the first route on the true south face of the mountain, on the right side, connecting with the southeast ridge. They climb in alpine style but suffer four days of open bivouacs and six days without food before returning. Hironobu Kamuro of Japan reaches the summit alone, via the normal route. 1982, 5 May – Three members – Philip Cornelissen, Rudi Van Snick, and Ang Rita Sherpa – of a Belgian-Nepali team reach the summit via the north-east ridge. A day later, four more climbers – Ang Jangbu Sherpa, Marnix Lefever, Lut Vivijs, and Jan Vanhees – summit also. Vivijs becomes the first woman to reach the summit.[13] 1982, 13 December – Two members (Akio Koizumi and Wangchu Shelpa) of the Japanese team led by Jun Arima of the Academic Alpine Club of Hokkaido University reach the summit. By the world calendar, winter begins 21 December, so this was not winter but a very-late-autumn-climb. sections.title: Climbing history
sections.content: Climbing history[edit] The unclimbed South Face of Dhaulagiri, seen from Poon Hill Dhaulagiri I in October 2002. The northeast ridge is the left skyline. Dhaulagiri was the penultimate eight-thousander to be summitted, and the final in Nepal. As its other routes are disproportionately dangerous, most ascents have followed the Northeast Ridge route of the first ascent, but climbs have been made from most directions. As of 2024, the two aspects which have repelled all attempts along their full length are the Northwest Ridge (though it has been climbed to the summit via the so-called "Pear" buttress) and the South Face. The latter is often regarded as one of the greatest remaining challenges in alpinism. As of 2007, there had been 358 successful ascents and 58 fatalities, which is a summit to a fatality rate of 16.2%.[1] Between 1950 and 2006, 2.88% of 2,016 expedition members and staff going above base camp on Dhaulagiri I died. On all 8,000 metre peaks in Nepal the death rate was 1.63%, ranging from 0.65% on Cho Oyu to 4.04% on Annapurna I and 3.05% on Manaslu.[2] Partial timeline[edit] 1950 – Dhaulagiri I reconnoitered by a French expedition led by Maurice Herzog. They do not see a feasible route and switch to Annapurna, where they make the first ascent of an 8000 m peak.[3] 1953–1958 – Five expeditions attempt the north face, or "Pear Buttress", route. 1959 – Austrian expedition led by Fritz Moravec makes the first attempt on the northeast ridge.[4] 1960 – Swiss-Austrian expedition led by Max Eiselin, successful ascent by Kurt Diemberger, Peter Diener, Ernst Forrer, Albin Schelbert, Nyima Dorje Sherpa, Nawang Dorje Sherpa on 13 May.[5] First Himalayan climb supported by the first prototype fixed-wing aircraft, which, after establishing the still standing record for highest fixed wing landing, eventually crashed in Hidden Valley north of the mountain during takeoff and was abandoned.[6] 1969 – American team led by Boyd Everett attempt southeast ridge; seven team members, including Everett, were killed in an avalanche.[7] 1970 – The second ascent, via the northeast ridge by a Japanese expedition led by Tokufu Ohta and Shoji Imanari. Tetsuji Kawada and Lhakpa Tenzing Sherpa reach the summit.[8] 1973 – American team led by James D. Morrissey makes the third ascent via the northeast ridge. Summit team: John Roskelley, Louis Reichardt, and Nawang Samden Sherpa.[9] 1975 – Japanese team led by Takashi Amemiya attempts southwest ridge (also known as the south pillar). Six are killed in an avalanche, including Norio Suzuki.[10] 1976 – Italian expedition makes the fourth ascent. 1977 – International team led by Reinhold Messner attempts the south face. 1978, spring: Amemiya returns with an expedition that puts five members on the summit via the southwest ridge—the first ascent not using the northeast ridge. One team member dies during the ascent. 1978, autumn – Seiko Tanaka of Japan leads successful climb of the very difficult southeast ridge. Four are killed during the ascent. French team attempts the southwest buttress (also called the "south buttress"), only reaches 7,200 m. 1980 – A four-man team consisting of Polish climbers Voytek Kurtyka, Ludwik Wiczyczynski, Frenchman René Ghilini, and Scotsman Alex MacIntyre climb the east face, topping out at 7,500 m on the northeast ridge. After a bivouac, they descend back to base camp in a storm. One week later they climb the mountain via the northeast ridge reaching the summit on 18 May.[11] 1981 – Yugoslav team reaches 7,950 m after putting up the first route on the true south face of the mountain, on the right side, connecting with the southeast ridge. They climb in alpine style but suffer four days of open bivouacs and six days without food before returning. Dhaulagiri, located in Nepal, is the seventh highest mountain in the world at 8,167 metres (26,795 ft) above sea level, and the highest mountain within the borders of a single country. Dhaulagiri I is also the highest point of the Gandaki river basin. It was first climbed on 13 May 1960 by a Swiss-Austrian-Nepali expedition.

query: The Well of Concubine Zhen, located within the Forbidden City, is named after a concubine of Emperor Guangxu who was tragically drowned there in 1900. It has since become a site of historical significance, reflecting the tumultuous events of the Qing Dynasty.
answer:
The **Well of Concubine Zhen** (珍妃井) is a significant historical site located within the Forbidden City in Beijing, China. It is named after Concubine Zhen of Emperor Guangxu, who was tragically drowned in this well in 1900 during the turmoil of the Boxer Rebellion. 

### Historical Significance:
- The well is situated at the northern end of the Ning Shou Palace, specifically inside the Zhen Shun Gate.
- Concubine Zhen was pushed into the well by eunuchs on the orders of Empress Dowager Cixi as the Qing Dynasty faced a crisis during the invasion of the Eight-Nation Alliance.
- After the fall of the Qing Dynasty, her remains were eventually retrieved and buried at the Western Suburbs of Beijing.

### Current Status:
Today, the well serves as a monument reflecting the tumultuous history of the Qing Dynasty and is part of the broader historical narrative of the Forbidden City. It stands as a reminder of the tragic events that unfolded during that era.

For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Well of Concubine Zhen](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%8F%8D%E5%A6%83%E4%BA%95).

sections.title: 简介
sections.content: 简介[编辑] 珍妃井原是宫中的一口普通水井。井眼上置有井口石，井口石两侧凿有小洞，用来穿入铁棍上锁。[1] 清朝光绪二十六年（1900年）八国联军进攻北京，慈禧太后和光绪帝西逃。临行前，慈禧太后将幽禁在景祺阁北小院的珍妃召到颐和轩，命太监崔玉贵和王德環等人将珍妃推入贞顺门内的这口井中溺死，该井因而得名“珍妃井”。[1] 光绪二十七年（1901年），銮驾返回北京，珍妃被追封为贵妃，珍妃的家人获准将珍妃的尸体从该井中打捞出来，安厝在北京西郊的田村，1913年迁葬清西陵的崇陵妃园寝。[1] 清朝宣统帝逊位之后，珍妃的姐姐瑾妃在此井北侧的贞顺门的东侧门房（穿堂东间）为珍妃设立了灵堂“怀远堂”，书“精卫通诚”匾，并制龛供奉“珍贵妃之神位”，以寄托对珍妃的哀思。[1]后人重新制作了此井的井口，不再使用。 如今，故宫博物院将怀远堂改设在珍妃井南侧的一座小房内，堂内仍布置有上述匾额及神龛。 ^ 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.3 引用错误：没有为名为zhenfeijing的参考文献提供内容

sections.content: 简介[编辑] 珍妃井原是宫中的一口普通水井。井眼上置有井口石，井口石两侧凿有小洞，用来穿入铁棍上锁。[1] 清朝光绪二十六年（1900年）八国联军进攻北京，慈禧太后和光绪帝西逃。临行前，慈禧太后将幽禁在景祺阁北小院的珍妃召到颐和轩，命太监崔玉贵和王德環等人将珍妃推入贞顺门内的这口井中溺死，该井因而得名“珍妃井”。[1] 光绪二十七年（1901年），銮驾返回北京，珍妃被追封为贵妃，珍妃的家人获准将珍妃的尸体从该井中打捞出来，安厝在北京西郊的田村，1913年迁葬清西陵的崇陵妃园寝。[1] 清朝宣统帝逊位之后，珍妃的姐姐瑾妃在此井北侧的贞顺门的东侧门房（穿堂东间）为珍妃设立了灵堂“怀远堂”，书“精卫通诚”匾，并制龛供奉“珍贵妃之神位”，以寄托对珍妃的哀思。[1]后人重新制作了此井的井口，不再使用。 如今，故宫博物院将怀远堂改设在珍妃井南侧的一座小房内，堂内仍布置有上述匾额及神龛。 ^ 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.3 引用错误：没有为名为zhenfeijing的参考文献提供内容

(August 2023) (Learn how and when to remove this message) Shillong was the capital of composite Assam during the British regime and for a quarter century in independent India until a separate State of Meghalaya was formed 1972. David Scott, the British civil servant of the East India Company, was the Agent of the Governor-General North East Frontier. During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British authorities felt the need for a road to connect Sylhet and Assam. The route was to traverse across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott overcame the difficulties his administration faced from the opposition of the Khasi Syiems – their chiefs and people. Impressed by the favourable cool climate of Khasi Hills, they negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra in 1829 for a sanatorium for the British. Thus began the consolidation of British interests in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills. In early 1829, a Khasis confederation mounted a serious uprising against British occupation. But by January 1833, their leader Tirot Sing surrendered to David Scott and was detained to Dacca (present-day Dhaka). A political agent was posted in Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee. But the British did not like the climate and facilities of Sohra and they moved to Shillong. "Ïewduh" is the biggest market in Shillong. The name "Shillong" was later adopted, as the location of the new town was below the Shillong Peak. In 1874, a separate Chief Commissionership was formed with Shillong as the seat of administration. The new administration included Sylhet, now a part of Bangladesh. Also included in the Chief Commissionership were the Naga Hills (present-day Nagaland), Lushai Hills (present-day Mizoram) as well as Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. Shillong was the capital of composite Assam till 1969 when the autonomous state of Meghalaya was formed. In January 1972, Meghalaya was made a full-fledged state.[1] The Shillong Municipal Board dates back to 1878, when a proclamation was issued constituting Shillong and its suburbs, including the villages of Mawkhar and Laban, into a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876. Inclusion of the villages of Mawkhar (S.E. Mawkhar, Jaiaw and part of Jhalupara and Mawprem) and Laban (Lumparing, Madan laban, Kench's Trace and Rilbong) within the Municipality of Shillong was agreed to by Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem under the agreement of 15 November 1878.[2] But, there is no trace of Shillong in the British era maps dating back to 1878, up to 1900. (August 2023) (Learn how and when to remove this message) Shillong was the capital of composite Assam during the British regime and for a quarter century in independent India until a separate State of Meghalaya was formed 1972. David Scott, the British civil servant of the East India Company, was the Agent of the Governor-General North East Frontier. During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British authorities felt the need for a road to connect Sylhet and Assam. The route was to traverse across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott overcame the difficulties his administration faced from the opposition of the Khasi Syiems – their chiefs and people. Impressed by the favourable cool climate of Khasi Hills, they negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra in 1829 for a sanatorium for the British. Thus began the consolidation of British interests in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills. In early 1829, a Khasis confederation mounted a serious uprising against British occupation. But by January 1833, their leader Tirot Sing surrendered to David Scott and was detained to Dacca (present-day Dhaka). A political agent was posted in Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee. But the British did not like the climate and facilities of Sohra and they moved to Shillong. "Ïewduh" is the biggest market in Shillong. The name "Shillong" was later adopted, as the location of the new town was below the Shillong Peak. In 1874, a separate Chief Commissionership was formed with Shillong as the seat of administration. The new administration included Sylhet, now a part of Bangladesh. Also included in the Chief Commissionership were the Naga Hills (present-day Nagaland), Lushai Hills (present-day Mizoram) as well as Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. Shillong was the capital of composite Assam till 1969 when the autonomous state of Meghalaya was formed. In January 1972, Meghalaya was made a full-fledged state.[1] The Shillong Municipal Board dates back to 1878, when a proclamation was issued constituting Shillong and its suburbs, including the villages of Mawkhar and Laban, into a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876. Inclusion of the villages of Mawkhar (S.E. Mawkhar, Jaiaw and part of Jhalupara and Mawprem) and Laban (Lumparing, Madan laban, Kench's Trace and Rilbong) within the Municipality of Shillong was agreed to by Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem under the agreement of 15 November 1878.[2] But, there is no trace of Shillong in the British era maps dating back to 1878, up to 1900. answer:
The Grand Buddha at Ling Shan (灵山大佛) is located on the north shore of Lake Tai, near Wuxi, Jiangsu, China. It is one of the largest Buddha statues in both China and the world. The statue is situated within the Lingshan Scenic Area, which is a popular tourist attraction.

### Key Information:
- **Name**: Grand Buddha at Ling Shan (灵山大佛)
- **Location**: Near Wuxi, Jiangsu, China
- **Category**: Attraction
- **Popularity Score**: 0.7 (indicating it is a well-visited site)
- **Wikipedia Link**: [Grand Buddha at Ling Shan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Buddha_at_Ling_Shan)

### Description:
The Grand Buddha is renowned for its impressive size and intricate design, making it a significant cultural and religious landmark. Visitors can enjoy panoramic views of the statue and the surrounding scenic area.

If you have any more questions or need further information, feel free to ask!

query: The Leshan Giant Buddha is a 71-meter tall stone statue carved into a cliff face, located at the confluence of the Min and Dadu Rivers in Sichuan Province, China. It is the largest and tallest stone Buddha statue in the world, facing Mount Emei.
answer:
The **Leshan Giant Buddha** (乐山大佛) is a remarkable 71-meter (233 ft) tall stone statue located in Sichuan Province, China, at the confluence of the Min and Dadu Rivers. Here are some key details about this iconic monument:

- **Construction**: The statue was built between 713 and 803 AD, carved out of a cliff face of Cretaceous red bed sandstones. It was commissioned by a Buddhist monk named Hai Tong, who believed that the statue would calm the turbulent waters that plagued shipping vessels in the area.

- **Design**: The statue faces Mount Emei, with the rivers flowing below its feet. It is recognized as the largest and tallest stone Buddha statue in the world and is also the tallest pre-modern statue globally.

- **Historical Significance**: The Leshan Giant Buddha has undergone various phases of construction and restoration over the centuries. It features a sophisticated drainage system to prevent weathering, which is still functional today.

- **Tourism**: The site is a popular tourist attraction, drawing visitors from around the world to admire its grandeur and historical significance.

For more information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_Giant_Buddha).

If you have any specific questions or need further details, feel free to ask!

(July 2023) (Learn how and when to remove this message) Construction started in 723 AD, led by a Chinese Buddhist monk named Hai Tong. He believed that Maitreya Buddha would calm the turbulent waters that constantly plagued the shipping vessels traveling down the river. When funding for the project was threatened, he is said to have gouged out his own eyes to show his piety and sincerity. After his death, however, the construction was delayed due to insufficient funding. The statue was only completed from the shoulders up at the time. Several years later, Hai Tong's disciples continued work on the statue with financial support from a local official named Zhangchou Jianxiong. Hai Tong's disciples continued the construction until the Knees, when construction was halted because Zhangchou JianXiang was called back to serve at the royal court in Chang'an. About 70 years later, Jiedushi Wei Gao continued to support and funded the project and the construction was finally completed by Hai Tong's disciples in 803. By the beginning of the Northern Song dynasty, the Leshan Giant Buddha had been damaged—the body was covered in moss, and the wooden pavilion had collapsed. During the reign of Song Renzong, the Giant Buddha was repaired once on a large scale and the wooden pavilion was rebuilt. Since then, the records of the destruction and reconstruction of the Buddha have been missing, and the original temple, Lingyun Temple, had been destroyed by war many times. Apparently, the massive construction resulted in so much stone being removed from the cliff face and deposited into the river below that the currents were indeed altered by the statue, making the water safe for passing ships.[citation needed] A sophisticated drainage system was incorporated into the Leshan Giant Buddha when it was built. It is still in working order. It includes drainage pipes carved into various places on the body, to carry away the water after the rains to reduce weathering. When the Giant Buddha was carved, a huge thirteen-story wood structure (similar to the one at the Rongxian Giant Buddha) was built to shelter it from rain and sunshine. This structure was destroyed and sacked by the Mongols during the wars at the end of the Yuan dynasty. From then on, the stone statue was exposed to the elements.

answer:
**小油坑 (Small Oil Pit)** is a volcanic vent located in **Yangmingshan National Park** in northern Taiwan, near the northwest foothills of **Qixing Mountain**. It serves as one of the trailheads for hiking in the area.

### Key Information:
- **Category**: Attraction
- **Elevation**: Approximately 805 meters
- **Popularity**: Moderate (0.7)

### Description:
小油坑 is known for its volcanic activity and scenic views, making it a popular spot for hikers and nature enthusiasts. The area features various hiking trails that offer panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.

### Additional Resources:
- [Wikipedia Article](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B0%8F%E6%B2%B9%E5%9D%91) for more detailed information.

If you have any specific questions or need further details, feel free to ask!

answer:
### Cuandixia (爨底下村)

**Overview:**
Cuandixia is a historic village dating from the Ming dynasty, located in Zhaitang, Mentougou District in Beijing, China. It is renowned for its well-preserved courtyard homes and serves as a popular tourist attraction.

**Historical Significance:**
- Founded during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) by members of the Han clan who migrated from Shanxi Province.
- The village prospered towards the end of the Qing Dynasty through trade in coal, fur, and grain.

**Attractions:**
- The village features traditional architecture and scenic views, making it a great spot for photography and cultural exploration.

**Visual Tags:**
- Tags associated with Cuandixia include exterior views, ground level perspectives, panoramic sights, and sunny weather conditions.

**Additional Information:**
- For more details, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuandixia).

If you have any specific questions or need further assistance regarding Cuandixia or other attractions, feel free to ask!

answer:
### Wanping Fortress (Wanping Castle)

**Overview:**
- **Name:** Wanping Fortress (宛平城)
- **Location:** Fengtai District, Beijing, China
- **Category:** Attraction / Monument
- **Historical Significance:** Built between 1638 and 1640 during the Ming Dynasty, Wanping Fortress was designed to defend Beijing against uprisings, particularly against Li Zicheng. It is also notable for its involvement in the Marco Polo Bridge Incident.

**Details:**
- **Historical Summary:** Wanping Fortress, also known as Wanping Castle, is a Ming Dynasty fortress or "walled city" in Fengtai District, Beijing. It was erected with the purpose of defending Beijing against peasant uprisings.
- **Transport:** It is served by Wanpingcheng station of Beijing Subway Line 16.
- **Visual Tags:** The fortress features various visual elements including panoramic views, cityscape, and is recognized as a significant monument in China.

**References:**
- For more information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanping_Fortress).

**Image:**
![Wanping Fortress](File:宛平城.jpg)

This fortress is a significant historical site reflecting China's architectural and military history during the Ming Dynasty. If you have any more questions or need further assistance, feel free to ask!

query: The Zhuhai Fisher Girl is a statue and landmark in Xianglu Bay, Zhuhai, China, completed in 1982. It symbolizes local culture and has become a significant part of the region's tourism industry.
answer:
The **Zhuhai Fisher Girl** is a prominent statue and landmark located in Xianglu Bay, Zhuhai, Guangdong, China. Here are some key details about this attraction:

- **Completion Year**: The statue was completed in **1982**.
- **Design**: It was designed by **Pan He** and is based on a local legend about a celestial being who disguised herself as a fisherwoman in the region. The statue depicts a young woman holding a pearl aloft, symbolizing beauty and vitality.
- **Cultural Significance**: The statue has become an iconic symbol of Zhuhai and plays a significant role in the local tourism industry. It was designated as a cultural relic in **2014**.
- **Location**: The statue stands on a boulder in Xianglu Bay and is accessible via a nearby boardwalk. The area around the statue is planned to be expanded into a mixed-purpose recreational area.

For more information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Zhuhai Fisher Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuhai_Fisher_Girl).

If you have any more questions or need further assistance, feel free to ask!

sections.title: Location and description
sections.content: Location and description[edit] The statue stands on a boulder in Xianglu Bay [zh]. It is located southeast of Zhuhai, and accessible via Qinglu Middle Road.[1] A boardwalk on the shore allows for close views,[2] and the nearby park, known as Lover's Road, contains ginkgo, white pine, elm, and locust trees.[3] Admission is free of charge.[2] The statue depicts a young woman, trouser leg rolled high, who is draped by a fishnet and holds a pearl high in the air with both hands up to the sky. The figure is adorned with jade bracelets and a pearl necklace.[4] She is described by the 21st Century Business Herald as "endowed with the image of classical beauty",[a] her strong and plump body combining the beauty of Ancient Greek sculpture with the "Oriental charm"[b] of depictions of the Buddha.[2] The statue, which symbolizes a vigorous and lively Zhuhai welcoming visitors from all over the world, stands 8.7 metres (29 ft) tall and is composed of seventy pieces of granite. sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] Zhuhai Fisher Girl (bottom left) along the coast of Zhuhai In 1979, as the Government of China prepared to create the Zhuhai Special Economic Zone, Wu Jianmin [zh] – later the first secretary of the municipal Chinese Communist Party committee – proposed the creation of a new statue that would become iconic of the nascent city. The committee reached out to the Department of Sculpture at the Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, seeking designs.[1] Initial drafts suggested erecting the sculpture at the Gongbei Port of Entry[2] and many of the early designs drew on imagery of male creators.[1] However, Pan He, an established sculptor and professor from the academy, proposed instead a design that reflected the historical importance of fishing in the region: a fisherwoman.[1] This idea drew on a local legend, which is recorded in several versions. According to one version, the daughter of the celestial Dragon King visited the Pearl River delta. Enamored by the beauty of the Zhuhai region, she disguised herself as a fisher girl and lived among the people there, weaving baskets and healing locals with her powers until she fell in love with a fellow fisherman named Haipeng. Their romance was interrupted by vicious rumors about the fisherwoman's true origins. Haipeng eventually confronted her about this and demanded that she give her magical pearl bracelets to him as proof of her love. She confirmed the rumors and explained that, if she removed even one of the pearls, she would die. As Haipeng turned to leave, the girl took off her bracelets, dying in his arms. Heartbroken and guilt-ridden, Haipeng set out to find a cure, eventually discovering from an elder that he would need to cultivate a special grass with his own blood. After years of toiling, Haipeng finally harvested enough to revive his beloved, turning her into a mortal. The two married and the fisher girl found a large pearl, which she gifted to the elder in gratitude.[a][3] Tourists at the statue This design was ultimately selected, to be erected in Xianglu Bay – then replete with wormwood and undergrowth.[2] The initial design depicted the woman holding a pearl before her, standing atop a fish.[4] In the final design, she holds the pearl aloft,[1] which the news website 163.com describes as giving a more pure and generous presentation. The fish, meanwhile, was removed from the design when its execution proved too difficult.[4] During the construction process, the sculpture became the subject of several discourses.[5] Opponents argued against the depiction of a fisherwoman, which was deemed immoral,[2] as well as the cost of erecting a large sculpture –  estimated at 200,000 yuan (equivalent to ¥1,230,000 in 2023) –  when the new city lacked adequate housing. Supporters, meanwhile, argued that the statue was necessary for Zhuhai to establish its own cultural identity, rather than be perceived as feeding off nearby Hong Kong and Macau.[1] Over time, as housing projects were completed and the special economic zone began to be realized, this controversy dwindled.[5] Installation of the statue was completed in 1982,[1] following which it was used as part of the zone's growing tourism industry.[5] Zhuhai Fisher Girl was recognized by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism as a cultural relic in 2014 after the definition of "relic" was expanded to include works created after the founding of the People's Republic of China. With this designation, no further changes could be made to the statue; however, plans were made in preparation to expand the surrounding area to create a 15,000-to-20,000-square-metre (160,000 to 220,000 sq ft) mixed-purpose recreational area. Drawing on the examples of the Macau Tower in Macau and the Oriental Pearl Tower in Shanghai, this proposal would see the bay around the statue reclaimed to create a modern tourist destination.[6] In 2005, to commemorate the 25th anniversary of Zhuhai's designation as a special economic zone, China Post issued a commemorative stamp titled "Beautiful Zhuhai" that depicts Zhuhai Fisher Girl.[7] Pan He completed a companion piece, Mother River (母亲河), in 2015 together with his son Pan Fen. Located along the Huangyuang River [zh] in Zhuhai's Doumen District, the statue depicts the young fisherwoman with her son. She has settled the land and is teaching her child to swim, even as she carries a fishing net and a pearl oyster.[1] ^ a b c d e f g .mw-parser-output cite.citation{font-style:inherit;word-wrap:break-word}.mw-parser-output .citation q{quotes:"\"""\"""'""'"}.mw-parser-output .citation:target{background-color:rgba(0,127,255,0.133)}.mw-parser-output .id-lock-free.id-lock-free a{background:url("//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/Lock-green.svg")right 0.1

sections.title: Location and description
sections.content: Location and description[edit] The statue stands on a boulder in Xianglu Bay [zh]. It is located southeast of Zhuhai, and accessible via Qinglu Middle Road.[1] A boardwalk on the shore allows for close views,[2] and the nearby park, known as Lover's Road, contains ginkgo, white pine, elm, and locust trees.[3] Admission is free of charge.[2] The statue depicts a young woman, trouser leg rolled high, who is draped by a fishnet and holds a pearl high in the air with both hands up to the sky. The figure is adorned with jade bracelets and a pearl necklace.[4] She is described by the 21st Century Business Herald as "endowed with the image of classical beauty",[a] her strong and plump body combining the beauty of Ancient Greek sculpture with the "Oriental charm"[b] of depictions of the Buddha.[2] The statue, which symbolizes a vigorous and lively Zhuhai welcoming visitors from all over the world, stands 8.7 metres (29 ft) tall and is composed of seventy pieces of granite. sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] Zhuhai Fisher Girl (bottom left) along the coast of Zhuhai In 1979, as the Government of China prepared to create the Zhuhai Special Economic Zone, Wu Jianmin [zh] – later the first secretary of the municipal Chinese Communist Party committee – proposed the creation of a new statue that would become iconic of the nascent city. The committee reached out to the Department of Sculpture at the Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, seeking designs.[1] Initial drafts suggested erecting the sculpture at the Gongbei Port of Entry[2] and many of the early designs drew on imagery of male creators.[1] However, Pan He, an established sculptor and professor from the academy, proposed instead a design that reflected the historical importance of fishing in the region: a fisherwoman.[1] This idea drew on a local legend, which is recorded in several versions. According to one version, the daughter of the celestial Dragon King visited the Pearl River delta. Enamored by the beauty of the Zhuhai region, she disguised herself as a fisher girl and lived among the people there, weaving baskets and healing locals with her powers until she fell in love with a fellow fisherman named Haipeng. Their romance was interrupted by vicious rumors about the fisherwoman's true origins. Haipeng eventually confronted her about this and demanded that she give her magical pearl bracelets to him as proof of her love. She confirmed the rumors and explained that, if she removed even one of the pearls, she would die. As Haipeng turned to leave, the girl took off her bracelets, dying in his arms. Heartbroken and guilt-ridden, Haipeng set out to find a cure, eventually discovering from an elder that he would need to cultivate a special grass with his own blood. After years of toiling, Haipeng finally harvested enough to revive his beloved, turning her into a mortal. The two married and the fisher girl found a large pearl, which she gifted to the elder in gratitude.[a][3] Tourists at the statue This design was ultimately selected, to be erected in Xianglu Bay – then replete with wormwood and undergrowth.[2] The initial design depicted the woman holding a pearl before her, standing atop a fish.[4] In the final design, she holds the pearl aloft,[1] which the news website 163.com describes as giving a more pure and generous presentation. The fish, meanwhile, was removed from the design when its execution proved too difficult.[4] During the construction process, the sculpture became the subject of several discourses.[5] Opponents argued against the depiction of a fisherwoman, which was deemed immoral,[2] as well as the cost of erecting a large sculpture –  estimated at 200,000 yuan (equivalent to ¥1,230,000 in 2023) –  when the new city lacked adequate housing. Supporters, meanwhile, argued that the statue was necessary for Zhuhai to establish its own cultural identity, rather than be perceived as feeding off nearby Hong Kong and Macau.[1] Over time, as housing projects were completed and the special economic zone began to be realized, this controversy dwindled.[5] Installation of the statue was completed in 1982,[1] following which it was used as part of the zone's growing tourism industry.[5] Zhuhai Fisher Girl was recognized by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism as a cultural relic in 2014 after the definition of "relic" was expanded to include works created after the founding of the People's Republic of China. With this designation, no further changes could be made to the statue; however, plans were made in preparation to expand the surrounding area to create a 15,000-to-20,000-square-metre (160,000 to 220,000 sq ft) mixed-purpose recreational area. Drawing on the examples of the Macau Tower in Macau and the Oriental Pearl Tower in Shanghai, this proposal would see the bay around the statue reclaimed to create a modern tourist destination.[6] In 2005, to commemorate the 25th anniversary of Zhuhai's designation as a special economic zone, China Post issued a commemorative stamp titled "Beautiful Zhuhai" that depicts Zhuhai Fisher Girl.[7] Pan He completed a companion piece, Mother River (母亲河), in 2015 together with his son Pan Fen. Located along the Huangyuang River [zh] in Zhuhai's Doumen District, the statue depicts the young fisherwoman with her son. She has settled the land and is teaching her child to swim, even as she carries a fishing net and a pearl oyster.[1] ^ a b c d e f g .mw-parser-output cite.citation{font-style:inherit;word-wrap:break-word}.mw-parser-output .citation q{quotes:"\"""\"""'""'"}.mw-parser-output .citation:target{background-color:rgba(0,127,255,0.133)}.mw-parser-output .id-lock-free.id-lock-free a{background:url("//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/Lock-green.svg")right 0.1

Commissioned ahead of the establishment of the Zhuhai Special Economic Zone, the statue was designed by Pan He based on a local legend about a celestial being who descended to the region to live as a simple fisherwoman. Though its cost was controversial, the statue was completed in 1982 and became part of the region's growing tourism industry. The statue was designated a cultural relic in 2014, and the following year the sculptor completed a companion piece with his son that depicts the fisher girl as a mother. A proposal has been made to expand the area around the statue into a mixed-purpose recreational area.

### Xidi (西递镇) - Overview

**Location**: Xidi is a town in Anhui Province, China, specifically under the jurisdiction of Huangshan City in Yi County.

**Cultural Significance**: 
- Xidi is renowned for its traditional architecture and rich cultural heritage. 
- It has been recognized as one of China's traditional villages and was included in the UNWTO's list of "Best Tourism Villages" in 2024.

**Historical Context**:
- Xidi was officially designated as a township-level administrative unit in China.
- The town is home to several ancient architectural complexes that are protected as national cultural heritage sites.

**Visual Tags**: The town is characterized by its exterior views, panoramic landscapes, and traditional Chinese architecture.

**Popularity**: Xidi is a popular tourist attraction, known for its scenic beauty and cultural heritage.

**Wikipedia Reference**: For more detailed information, you can visit the [Wikipedia page for Xidi](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%A5%BF%E9%80%92%E9%95%87).

### Conclusion
Xidi is a culturally rich destination that showcases traditional Chinese architecture and is recognized for its significance in tourism. If you're interested in exploring historical villages in China, Xidi is a must-visit location.

query: Тавдинские пещеры, located in the Altai region, are a large system of karst caves named after the nearby village of Tavda. The caves extend approximately 5 km and are popular among tourists, with some entrances equipped for easy access.
answer:
### Тавдинские пещеры (Tavdin Caves)

**Location:** Altai region, Russia  
**Category:** Attraction  
**Popularity:** Moderate (0.7)

**Description:**  
Тавдинские пещеры, также известные как Талдинские пещеры, представляют собой обширную систему карстовых пещер, расположенных на левом берегу реки Катунь в Алтайском районе. Длина пещер составляет около 5 км, и они получили свое название от близлежащей деревни Тавда. Входы в пещеры находятся в отвесных скалах и утесах, и большинство из них легко доступны. 

Из-за популярности среди туристов некоторые входы оборудованы деревянными ступенями, а в наиболее посещаемых пещерах проведено освещение. Многие пещеры имеют несколько входов и соединены между собой, образуя большую взаимосвязанную систему. Вход в легкодоступные пещеры оборудован турникетами и является платным.

**Notable Features:**

(7 марта 2025) Тавдинская карстовая арка Уникальна Тавдинская карстовая арка. Она представляет редкую форму — остаток свода карстового туннеля или пещеры, имевший первоначально вид широкого пролёта — моста, а позднее — арки. Тавдинская арка находится на высоте около 80 метров над уровнем воды реки Катунь. Ширина сквозного отверстия арки колеблется от 3 до 13 метров, высота — от 3 до 5 метров. Свод арки, толщиной 5 метров, покрыт редкой травяной растительностью и соснами. С 1996 г. Тавдинская карстовая арка имеет статус памятника природы.

result.historical_summary: Тавдинские или Талдинские пещеры — массив из большого числа пещер карстового происхождения в Алтайском районе Алтайского края, на левом берегу Катуни. Своё название пещеры получили от названия деревни Тавда, ранее располагавшейся неподалёку от этих мест. Протяжённость скал с пещерами составляет около 5 км. Входы в пещеры находятся в отвесных скалах и утесах, большая часть из которых легко доступна. В связи с популярностью и большой посещаемостью этого места туристами, некоторые входы даже оборудованы деревянными ступенями, в самые посещаемые туристами пещеры проведён свет. Многие пещеры имеют по несколько входов и соединяются друг с другом, образуя большую взаимосвязанную систему. Вход в легкодоступные пещеры оборудован турникетами и является платным.

wikipedia.title: 萩城
wikipedia.extract: Hagi Castle  is a Japanese castle located in the city of Hagi, Yamaguchi Prefecture, in the San'yō region of Japan. Built in 1604 at the beginning of the Edo period as the main castle of the Mōri clan, it served as the seat of the Chōshū Domain for over 250 years until 1863. It was demolished in 1874 shortly after the Meiji Restoration. Its ruins were designated a National Historic Site in 1924. Hagi Castle has been designed as a component of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining, which received UNESCO World Heritage Site status in 2015.

The Yoshimi were retainers of the Ōuchi clan, who were shugo of the provinces on Nagato and Suō from the late Kamakura period. In the mid-Muromachi period, the Ōuchi were overthrown by their own general, Sue Harukata, who was in turn defeated by the Mōri clan. Mōri Motonari was originally a minor warlord from Aki Province, but after defeating Sue Harutaka and later the Amago clan of Izumo Province, rose to become the ruler of most of the Chugoku region of western Japan. Under his grandson, Mōri Terumoto and with the support of Kikkawa Motoharu and Kobayakawa Takakage, the Mōri continued to expand, but eventually came into conflict with Oda Nobunaga, who general Hashiba Hideyoshi and gradually were forced back into the western half of the Chugoku region. Nobunaga was assassinated before the Mōri could be completely defeated, and agreed to become vassals of his successor, Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Under Toyotomi rule, the Mōri constructed Hiroshima Castle as their main stronghold. After the death of Hideyoshi, the Mōri supported his son, Toyotomi Hideyori, at the 1600 Battle of Sekigahara against Tokugawa Ieyasu. However, the Mōri did not actually participate in any combat during that battle, as Kikkawa Hiroie was in secret communication with the Tokugawa forces and prevented the Mōri army from receiving orders to move forward. After the battle and the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate, Tokugawa Ieyasu betrayed his agreement with the Mōri and seized two-thirds of their holdings, including their home province of Aki. Forced back to only Nagato and Suō, the Mōri needed a new stronghold. Initially they petitioned to be allowed to construct their stronghold in either Yamaguchi or Hōfu, which were on the strategic Sanyōdō highway which connected Kyoto with Kyushu. However, the shogunate rejected these proposals and ordered that they build their stronghold at Hagi, which was at the time only a small fishing village, distant from important roads and was a swampy area hemmed in by hills and rivers. Construction of Hagi Castle began in 1604 and was completed in 1608. Although Chōshū Domain played a major role in the history of Bakumatsu Japan and the Meiji restoration, Hagi Castle was not the site of any major conflict. In 1863, the Mōri clan moved their seat from Hagi Castle to Yamaguchi Castle for fear of attack by foreign naval forces following the Shimonoseki campaign. Destruction and ruins[edit] In 1874, most of the castle structures were demolished by order of the new Meiji government and some moats were reclaimed.[1] However, the stone walls of central area and hilltop area remain largely intact, and the outer gate and a corner turret was later restored. The ruins were declared a National Historic Site in 1951, as was Hagi Castle Town in 1967.[2] Mount Shigetsu [3] was designated a National Natural Monument in 1971. In 2006, Hagi Castle was selected as one of Japan's Top 100 Castles by the Japan Castle Foundation in 2006.[4] It was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on July 5, 2015, as part of the Sites of Japan’s Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining.
